Module 2: Data Visualization Lecture Your browser does not support PDFs. Download the PDF. Lab Introduction Description of the lab Welcome to the lab for Genome Visualization! This lab will introduce you to the Integrative Genomics Viewer, a powerful desktop application for viewing many kinds of genomic data, including data for DNA sequencing, RNA sequencing, microarrays, epigenetics, and copy number alteration. You will also get an introduction to the UCSC Genome Browser, a full featured web application integrating rich annotation sources. Many thanks to Dr. Rob Syme and previous instructors for their material for this lab. After this lab, you will be able to: Visualize a variety of genomic data Quickly navigate around the genome Visualize HTS read alignments Validate SNP calls and structural re-arrangements by eye Things to know before you start: The lab may take between 1-2 hours, depending on your familiarity with genome browsing. Don’t worry if you don’t complete the lab! It is available for you to complete later. There are a few thought-provoking Questions or Notes pertaining to sections of the lab. These are optional, and may take more time, but are meant to help you better understand the visualizations you are seeing. Requirements Integrative Genomics Viewer Ability to run Java Data Set for IGV Chromosome 21:19,000,000-20,000,000 HCC1143.normal.21.19M-20M.bam HCC1143.normal.21.19M-20M.bam.bai Visualization Part 1: Getting Familiar with IGV We will be visualizing read alignments using the Integrative Genomics Viewer. First, lets familiarize ourselves with it. The IGV Interface Load a Genome and Data Tracks By default, IGV loads Human hg38 as the reference genome. If you work with another version of the human genome, or another organism altogether, you can change the genome by clicking the drop down menu in the upper-left. For the first part of this lab, we’ll be using Human hg19. Go to (Genomes -> Download hosted genomes -> hg19) and leave the radio buttons set to “remote” options. We will also load additional tracks from Server (File -> Load from Server): Ensembl genes (or your favourite source of gene annotations) GC Percentage Navigation You should see listing of chromosomes in this reference genome. Click on 1, for chromosome 1. Navigate to chr1:10,000-11,000 by entering this into the location field (in the top-left corner of the interface) and clicking Go or pressing Enter/Return on your keyboard. This shows a window of chromosome 1 that is 1,000 base pairs wide and beginning at position 10,000. You can also zoom by clicking and dragging in the region of the position bar. IGV displays the sequence of letters in a genome as a sequence of colours (e.g. A = green). This makes repetitive sequences, like the ones found at the start of this region, easy to identify. You can navigate to a gene of interest by typing it in the same box the genomic coordinates are in and pressing Enter/Return. Try it for your favourite gene, or BRCA1 if you can’t decide. Genes are represented as lines and boxes. Lines represent intronic regions, and boxes represent exonic regions. The arrows indicate the strand on which the gene lies. When loaded, tracks are stacked on top of each other. You can identify which track is which by consulting the label to the left of each track. Region Lists Sometimes it’s really useful to save where you are, or to load regions of interest. For this purpose, there is a Region Navigator in IGV. To access it, click Regions > Region Navigator. While you browse around the genome, you can save some bookmarks by pressing the Add button at any time. Loading Read Alignments We will visualize alignments from the breast cancer cell line HCC1143. For speed, only a small portion of chr21 will be loaded (19M:20M). HCC1143 Alignments to hg19: HCC1143.normal.21.19M-20M.bam HCC1143.normal.21.19M-20M.bam.bai Note These are the same files listed at the top of tutorial. Copy the files to your local drive, and in IGV choose File > Load from File, select the bam file, and click OK. Note that the bam and index files must be in the same directory for IGV to load these properly, but only the bam file (not the bam.bai file) needs to be loaded into IGV. Visualizing Read Alignments Navigate to a narrow window on chromosome 21: “chr21:19,480,041-19,480,386”. IGV lets you group, sort, and color alignments to better visualize the data. To start our exploration, right click on the track name, and select the following options: Sort alignments by “start location” Group alignments by “pair orientation” Experiment with the various settings by right clicking the read alignment track and toggling the options. Think about which would be best for specific tasks (e.g. quality control, SNP calling, CNV finding). You will see reads represented by grey or white bars stacked on top of each other, where they were aligned to the reference genome. The reads are pointed to indicate their orientation (i.e. the strand on which they are mapped). Individual bases are only colored if they are a mismatch to the reference. The transparacy of the mismatched bases corresponds to the base quality. Mouse over any read and notice that a lot of information is available. To toggle read display from “hover” to “click”, select the yellow box at the top of the window and change the setting. Once you select a read, a pop-up window shows quality metrics and other information about that read. Visualization Part 2: Inspecting SNPs, SNVs, and SVs Neighbouring Somatic SNV and Germline SNP Questions: What does “Shade base by quality” do? How might this be helpful? Distinguishes high-quality bases from lower quality bases. If the T alternate allele was predominantly light/transparent, we wouldn’t be very confident that it is a probable SNV. The only light-colored T in this example is at the very end of a read, where base quality is generally lower. How does “Color by read strand” help? Lets us see that the T alternate allele is present on both forward and reverse sequencing reads. If it was present on only forward reads or only reverse reads, that could indicate a sequencing artifact as opposed to a probable SNV. Homopolymer Repeat with Indel Question: Is the “T” likely a valid SNV? What evidence suggests it is or isn’t? Probably not. 6/36 reads show a T at this positition (numbers obtained by clicking/hovering on the coverage track block at this position), and 4 of those 6 are light colored (low quality). Additionally, only forward (red) reads have the T alternate allele, indicating a strand bias sequencing error. Coverage by GC Question: Does the coverage correspond to the GC content? Yes! Read coverage is low where GC content of the reference genome is very low (and also very high, but in these data the low coverage effect is easier to see). Seqeuencing technologies are not perfect and have biases, meaning not all regions of the genome are covered equally. You can read more about the effect of GC content on short-read sequencing coverage here. Low Mapping Quality Question: Why do repeat elements affect mapping quality? Repeat elements, like LINEs (long interspersed nuclear elements), are retrotransposons found throughout the genome. Because these sequences are repeated in many different locations, when a read aligns to part of this sequence, it can often map equally well to multiple locations in the genome. This is not helpful, so aligners generally give low mapping quality scores reads that do not map uniquely to one location (i.e. 0; the reads will also be white instead of grey in IGV). Homozygous Deletion Question: What other track provides evidence of a deletion at this location? The coverage track drops down to zero at the same location as the gap in sequencing reads. Visualization Part 3: Visualizing Long Reads Cleaning up Sequencing Error Noise Question: What does the abundance of dashed lines and purple “I”s tell us about the types of errors produced by nanopore sequencing? Nanopore sequencing is prone to insertions and deletions. “I”s are insertions and the dashed lines are deletions, relative to the reference genome. Viewing Variants Question: Some of the coloring options we used for viewing the previous sample (HCC1143) are not available for this NA12878 bam, such as View as pairs and Color alignments by insert size and pair orientation. Why is this? Nanopore sequencing doesn’t do paired read sequencing! Instead, long fragments of DNA are pulled through pores and are sequenced until the end of the fragment (or until the pore wears out). Reads are considered to be independent from each other in this regard. This is different from short-read sequencing platforms like Illumina that sequence both ends of a DNA fragment but are usually unable to sequence the middle segment.

Open slides in a new tab Lab Garbage In, Garbage Out: Auditing Your Nanopore Reads Introduction: Meet Your Dataset For the next two days you will follow one real dataset from raw reads to variants. It is BAL_1a, a wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker’s yeast) isolate sequenced on an Oxford Nanopore MinION (run ERR8562432, R9.4.1 flow cell). The sequencing is not subsampled: you work with every read, as in a real project. The case. For two days you are a detective. The suspect is a wolf (our isolate, BAL_1a): a wild yeast from rotten wood on Bawangling Mountain, Hainan, China. You compare it with a corgi (S288C, the lab-bred reference strain). Two questions run through the labs. Does the wolf differ in genes for ethanol fermentation? Does it differ in genes for stress response? First things first: is the evidence, the reads, good enough to use? Today you do the first computational step, quality control (QC): measuring how good the data are before you spend hours using them. By the end of this lab you will have: built your own project folders on the cluster and downloaded the data, run sequali, a QC tool for long reads, and read its report, thought through a read-filtering step (without running it), submitted the genome assembly job (Flye) that the next module’s lecture will explain. The lab has these parts: Part 0: where we are, and the anatomy of a Slurm script Part 1: the nano routine, and your project folders Part 2: download the reads and the reference Part 3: check that your tools work Part 4: run sequali on the raw reads Part 5: copy the report to your laptop and read it Part 6: think it through, filtering Part 7: submit the assembly, then lunch Bonus: short-read QC in R (optional) Where we are in the workflow This lab covers the highlighted stage, read QC. Read this once A script (.sh file) is a text file of commands. In this lab you copy each script from this page, save it with nano, and run it. Some scripts run on the login node (the computer you land on when you log in; only quick jobs go here) with bash. Others go to a compute node (where the real work happens) through Slurm with sbatch. Every step below tells you which one to use. Part 0: Where We Are and How a Script Is Built You met Slurm in the orientation. Here is the anatomy once more, using a tiny example. You do not need to run this one. anatomy_example.sh #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=anatomy #SBATCH --account=def-sponsor00 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2 #SBATCH --mem=4000M #SBATCH --time=0:10:00 # This is a comment. The shell ignores it. echo "Hello from $(hostname)" What each argument does #SBATCH lines and set-up: see Lab 3, script 04. The #SBATCH lines are also explained in the bullets below and in Question 2. This box covers only what is specific to this example. Argument What it does Why this value #!/bin/bash The first line, starting with #!, names the program that runs the file (the “shebang”). All scripts in this lab are bash scripts. echo "Hello from $(hostname)" echo prints text. hostname prints the name of the computer; $( ) pastes its output into the text. A harmless command, so you can see which computer ran the job. Line 1, #!/bin/bash, is the shebang: it says “run this file with the bash shell”. Lines starting with #SBATCH are requests to Slurm: CPUs, memory (--mem), maximum run time (--time) and your account. Slurm reads them before it runs anything. Other lines starting with # are comments, notes for humans. The remaining lines are the commands that run. Every script in this lab also starts with the same few lines after the #SBATCH block: set -e (stop at the first error, so one failure does not hide behind later output), WORK=... (where your project lives) and cd "$WORK" (go there). Each script ends with echo lines that print the names of the files it made. Question 1: In the example, how much memory and how much time does the job request? What do you expect to happen if the job needs more of either? Answer It requests 4000 MB of memory (--mem=4000M) and 10 minutes (--time=0:10:00), with 2 CPUs. Slurm enforces these limits: a job that runs past its time or memory is stopped (cancelled) by Slurm, and the log shows a time-limit or out-of-memory message. Step 2: Read the report Two QC terms to keep in mind before you look: A Phred quality score (Q) says how likely a base is wrong: Q = −10 × log₁₀(probability of error). Q10 means 90% correct, Q20 99%, Q30 99.9%. The mean read quality is a read’s average quality. It is best computed by averaging the error probabilities and converting back, not by averaging the Q numbers, because a few very bad bases matter more than the Q average suggests. The read length distribution is how many reads there are of each length (a histogram). It shows whether the library is mostly long reads or full of short fragments. The read N50 is the length such that half of all bases sit in reads at least that long. sequali shows it in the Contiguity table of its “Sequence length distribution” section. Open the report in your browser and answer Questions 4-9. Question 4: In sequali’s summary table, how many reads (Total reads) and bases (Total bases) are there, and what is the Mean length? Check the mean by dividing the bases by the number of reads. Given a yeast genome of about 12 Mb, roughly how many times is each base covered (the coverage)? Answer Total reads 22,964; Total bases 448,028,488; Mean length 19,510 bp (test run of this lab’s script, sequali 1.0.1, 2026-10-11; your numbers should match). Check: 448,028,488 ÷ 22,964 = 19,510 bp. Coverage = total bases ÷ genome size = 448 Mb ÷ about 12 Mb, so roughly 37×. If your counts differ, the download may be incomplete: tell an instructor. Question 5: In the “Per sequence average quality scores” histogram, where is the peak? What percentage of reads are at or above Q10 and at or above Q20 (see the table above the plot)? Convert the peak Q to a percentage accuracy using the Q10 = 90%, Q20 = 99% rule. What kinds of errors will remain in an assembly built from these reads? Answer The histogram peaks at Q9 (43.6% of reads). 10.4% of reads are at or above Q10, and none reach Q20 (test run of this lab’s script, sequali 1.0.1, 2026-10-11; your numbers should match). Q9 means about a 13% chance that a base is wrong, so roughly 87% accuracy, or about 1 error in every 8 bases. These are older (2017-18) R9.4.1 reads, far less accurate than Illumina reads (Q30 and above) or current ONT chemistry. Why the averaging matters: sequali averages each read’s error probabilities, as we do. If you averaged the Q numbers instead, the median read would look like Q13 rather than Q9, and 97% of reads would appear to be at or above Q10 instead of 10% (checked on all 22,964 reads). What stays in an assembly: random errors are outvoted when many reads cover the same position, but systematic errors, mainly insertions and deletions in homopolymers (runs of the same base), recur across reads and so are not simply outvoted. That is why polishers such as medaka use trained models (Module 4). Question 6: In the “Sequence length distribution” section, what is the read N50 (Contiguity table)? Is it larger or smaller than sequali’s mean length, and why? Answer Read N50 = 31,865 bp (N90 10,459 bp; median read length 14,801 bp) (test run of this lab’s script, sequali 1.0.1, 2026-10-11; your numbers should match). It is larger than the mean length (19,510 bp) because N50 is weighted by bases: half of all bases sit in reads of 31.9 kb or longer, so the long reads, which carry most of the bases, pull it up, while the many shorter reads pull the mean down. A read N50 this far above the length of yeast’s common repeats (for example the Ty retrotransposons, about 6 kb) is good news for assembly, because long reads can span repeats. Question 7: Look at the plot of quality along the read (position in read on the x-axis). Is quality stable from the start of the reads to the end, or does it change? Compare this with what you learned about Illumina reads on day 1. Answer Quality is essentially flat along the reads, at a mean of about Q8 to Q8.5 (test run of this lab’s script, sequali 1.0.1, 2026-10-11; your numbers should match). It is slightly lower in the first ~25 bases, and lower again in the last few dozen bases of each read (visible in the plot anchored to the read end). The far right of the plot is noisy because very few reads are longer than 100 kb. There is no steady decline toward the 3′ end as in Illumina reads, where the strands in each cluster drift out of step (phasing) cycle after cycle. For ONT, the useful view is the spread of quality between reads (Question 5), not a 3′ drop. Question 8: In “Per position N content”, what is the highest percentage of N at any position? What is an N, and what would a high N count tell you about the reads? Answer 0%: there is not a single N in the 448 Mb (test run of this lab’s script, sequali 1.0.1, 2026-10-11; your numbers should match). An N is an ambiguous base, a position where the basecaller could not decide between A, C, G and T. ONT basecallers always output a base; when they are unsure, the uncertainty shows up as a low quality score instead of an N. Many Ns (more common in short-read data) would make reads suspect and point to a problem with the run or basecalling. Question 9: Look at the nucleotide (A, C, G, T) proportions along the reads and at the GC content. Are the proportions steady along the reads? Is the GC content near what we expect for S. cerevisiae, about 38% (the GC of the polished assembly, 38.16%; QUAST report.txt, benchmark run)? Question 11: What would an assembly gain from filtering, and what would it lose? Answer Gain: a cleaner input, since the worst reads (short and low quality) are removed, and in some cases less run time and fewer misleading reads. Lose: coverage. Question 13: In the quality-by-cycle plot, around which cycle does the bottom of the box (the worst quarter of reads) drop below the dashed Q30 line? Is the drop earlier and sharper in R1 or R2? Answer The bottom of the box (25th percentile) drops below Q30 at about cycle 63 in R1 and about cycle 57 in R2, so R2 is earlier and sharper. The medians stay above Q30 (R1 ends at Q33, R2 at Q31). (From a test run of this script, 2026-10-11; the plots agree.) Illumina quality declines toward the 3′ end as the strands in each cluster drift out of step (phasing). R2 is usually worse than R1. A study across many labs and instruments found that longer DNA fragments are a major reason (Tan et al. 2019, Scientific Reports). Question 14: Compare R1 and R2 in the read-quality histogram. Which has more low-quality reads, and what would you do with that information? Answer R2 has more low-quality reads. With the mean read quality averaged as error probabilities (as in this plot), 30.4% of R2 reads are below Q20, against 24.2% of R1 reads (20,000 reads per file; from a test run of this script, 2026-10-11). A simple average of the Q values hides much of this: it puts only 9.9% (R2) and 4.8% (R1) below Q20, because a few very bad bases weigh far more as error probabilities than as Q numbers. For short reads, trimming the low-quality 3′ ends or removing poor reads is standard before alignment or assembly, because Illumina reads are short and trimming costs little. Question 15: Look at the base-composition plot. Is the percentage of A, C, G and T flat across cycles? What do any bumps at the start of the read suggest? Answer The composition is not flat for about the first 12 cycles, then it is flat at roughly A 22%, C 27%, G 28% and T 22%. N stays at or below 0.9% at every cycle (from a test run of this script, 2026-10-11). These example reads are human RNA-seq, and the bias in the first ~12 cycles is the classic pattern of random-hexamer priming during library prep, not a property of the genome. A rise in N at some cycle would point to a sequencing problem at that cycle.

Question 4: What is the mean coverage that Flye reports? Compare it with the coverage you calculated in Lab 3 (Question 4). Why does enough coverage matter for an assembly? Answer 37× (flye.log, “Mean coverage”) (workshop cluster test run, 2026-10-18, Flye 2.9.6-b1802, 8 CPUs; yours may differ slightly). Benchmark expectation: about 37×, the same as the Lab 3 calculation (448 Mb of reads ÷ about 12 Mb; ENA ERR8562432). Flye needs every position covered by several overlapping reads: coverage lets the reads outvote each other’s errors (systematic errors, such as those in homopolymers, can survive the vote, which is why we polish) and bridge the gaps between neighbouring pieces. With long reads, 30-50× is a good depth for a small genome like yeast (Module 4 lecture). Part 2: Polishing with medaka Why polish? Flye’s assembly is built from reads that are only about 87% accurate (Lab 3, Question 5). Flye’s own three internal polishing rounds (--iterations 3) fix many errors, but some remain, mostly indels (small insertions or deletions) in homopolymers (runs of the same base). Polishing corrects them with the reads: the reads are aligned to the draft, and at each position the reads “vote” for the base that most of them support (the consensus). medaka does the voting with a trained neural-network model instead of a simple majority, because it has learned how nanopore errors look. What: runs medaka on your assembly, with your raw reads. Why: correct the base errors in the draft before we measure its quality. Expected output: results/ERR8562432/polishing/consensus.fasta, the polished assembly. It runs for about 3-9 minutes. Annotation has two parts: Structural annotation says where the genes are: a gene model is a predicted gene structure (gene, mRNA, exons, coding sequence). We supply the result of funannotate, a gene-prediction pipeline. In yeast, most genes have no introns (about 5% do) and genes are packed closely, so prediction is easier than in larger eukaryotes. Functional annotation says what the genes do. We supply the result of eggNOG-mapper, which compares each predicted protein with a database of gene families (families of orthologs, genes in different species that descend from one ancestral gene) and transfers the best-matching gene’s name and function. These files describe the instructor’s assembly, not yours The annotation was made on the benchmark polished assembly (contig names such as contig_1). Your own assembly has its own contigs, so the coordinates and contig names in these files will not match yours. For learning how to read an annotation this does not matter. The structural annotation is a GFF3 file: a tab-separated text file with one feature per line, like an address book for the genome. Its nine columns are: Column Name Example 1 seqid (the contig) contig_1 2 source (the program) funannotate 3 type (what kind of feature) gene, mRNA, exon, CDS, tRNA 4-5 start, end 2782, 3705 6 score . How do the numbers of gene, mRNA and tRNA lines relate to each other? There are 14,159 CDS lines for 6,191 mRNA lines, about 2.3 per gene; a gene without introns would have just one. Is that what you expect for yeast, and what could explain it? (Hint: think about BUSCO’s internal stop codons in Part 5.) To see a concrete case, look at the output of the fourth command above, which shows the pieces of FUN_003391-T1, eggNOG’s best match for the well-known gene ADH1. Answer 6,443 gene, 6,191 mRNA, 252 tRNA, 14,411 exon and 14,159 CDS lines (targeted counts on ERR8562432_funannotate.gff3). 6,191 + 252 = 6,443: every gene is either a protein-coding gene (it has an mRNA) or a tRNA gene (a gene for a transfer RNA). A CDS (coding sequence) is the part of an exon that is translated into protein. A gene split by introns gets one exon line and one CDS line per piece. The mismatch is the point of the question. Only about 5% of yeast genes have introns, yet about two-thirds of the predicted models (4,019 of 6,191) have more than one CDS piece, and many of the implied introns are very short (some only 10-30 bp). The ADH1 model, for example, is predicted in 2 CDS pieces (contig_10:910,903-911,054 and 911,252-912,284), although ADH1 is not expected to contain an intron. The most likely explanation (an inference, not proven) is the small errors left in the assembly: a missing or extra base in a homopolymer shifts the reading frame, and the gene predictor can “repair” the frame by adding a short intron across the error. BUSCO shows the same problem from another side: 157 complete genes contain internal stop codons. To confirm it, you would compare these models with the S288C annotation or polish with accurate short reads. The lesson: an annotation is only as good as the assembly under it, so always compare it with what you know about the species. The R7.3 assembly has C:43.7% (S 43.4%, D 0.3%), F 2.6%, M 53.7% (QUAST report.txt and short_summary, ERR1539006): more than half of the genes are missing, even though that assembly is about 10 Mb long, close to the genome size. The contrast shows that read quality matters: older, noisier reads give broken genes and a fragmented assembly (431 contigs, N50 28.6 kb), and BUSCO catches this even when the total length looks reasonable. Question 11: About 4% of the genes are “duplicated” (D). What could that mean? Answer Workshop cluster test run: D = 4.6%, which is 107 genes (short_summary). Two kinds of explanation: (1) biological: the isolate really carries two copies of that gene, for example paralogs (genes related by an ancient duplication), or a region copied in this isolate; (2) technical: the assembly contains the same stretch of the genome twice, for example a repeated region assembled into two contigs. BUSCO alone cannot separate them. You would check where the two copies lie, and compare with the reference. Compare with the older assembly: its D was only 0.3%, but that is because most of its genes were missing. Question 12: BUSCO notes that some complete genes contain internal stop codons. How many, and what does this tell you about the remaining errors in the assembly? Answer Workshop cluster test run: 155 of the 2,311 complete BUSCOs (E = 6.7%) contain an internal stop codon (short_summary). A real gene should not have a stop codon in the middle. The likely cause is a residual error from the nanopore reads, mostly an insertion or deletion in a homopolymer, which shifts the reading frame and creates a stop. So even after Flye and medaka, a small number of base errors remain, which BUSCO exposes although N50 and the gene count cannot. Polishing with accurate short reads (a hybrid approach) would fix many of them. Be careful, though: BUSCO’s own gene alignments are imperfect, and a few flagged genes may be real pseudogenes. Also, the June benchmark assembly (the supplied one) was polished without -m, so with medaka’s default model (r1041_e82_400bps_sup_v5.2.0 in medaka 2.2.2) for newer R10.4.1 flow cells; part of the remaining errors may come from that mismatch. GT:GQ 1:4: on chromosome I at position 63, the reference has T and the sample has C. GT=1 means that the sample carries the alternate allele (C). Question 2: Look at the genotypes in the first records. Every one is GT=1, never 0/1, and there is no column for read depth or for the fraction of reads that carry the variant. What does this tell you about the type of caller, and what can this VCF not tell you? Answer GT=1 (a single allele, not a pair like 0/1) is the notation for a haploid genotype. medaka_variant is a haploid caller: it assumes one copy of each chromosome, so each position is either the reference or the alternate allele. The consequence is that this file cannot report heterozygosity (two different alleles in one individual), and medaka.vcf does not record how many reads support each allele (the header declares only GT and GQ). medaka also writes medaka.annotated.vcf, which adds read depth (DP) and the reads supporting each allele (SR); we filter the plain medaka.vcf, as in the workshop pipeline. In Part 5 you count the reads yourself in IGV. For BAL_1a, a homozygous diploid (ScRAP: 2n, homozygous), both copies carry the same base, so GT=1 is a fitting model (Part 5). We keep the variants with QUAL >= 20 (at most about a 1% chance of being wrong) using bcftools, a standard toolkit for VCF files. bcftools filter -i 'QUAL >= 20' includes only the records that pass this test. bcftools stats then writes a summary table that includes the counts of SNVs and indels, and the transition/transversion ratio (see Question 5). A transition is a change within the purines (A↔︎G) or within the pyrimidines (C↔︎T); a transversion is any other single-base change. If every base change were equally likely, what ratio would you expect, and what do you conclude? Answer Ts/Tv = 2.98: 84,059 transitions and 28,210 transversions (bcftools stats on filtered.vcf, workshop cluster test run; the two add up to the 112,269 SNVs). For random changes, each base can change into one transition and two transversions, so the ratio would be about 0.5. A ratio far above 0.5 is the signature of real variants, because mutations that are transitions are biologically more frequent than transversions. The annotation that we supplied (Lab 4) describes the instructor’s assembly, with contigs named contig_1, contig_2, and so on. To see a variant together with the annotation of the assembly, you must convert its position from the reference to the assembly. This is called liftover. It places each call, with its snpEff annotation, on the coordinates of the isolate’s own assembly, so you can see it next to the gene models made on that assembly. Answer The chain file only has entries for the blocks where the assembly aligned to the reference. A variant whose reference position lies outside an aligned block has no “address” on the assembly and cannot be moved. That happens where the assembly is missing sequence that the reference has (the isolate lacks it, or the assembler left it out: repeats, the ribosomal DNA array, chromosome ends), and where the two genomes differ so much that minimap2 could not align them. Also, the preset -x asm5 is meant for genomes that differ by well under 1%, but BAL_1a differs from S288C by about 1%, so alignments are broken more often in diverged regions, which probably adds to the failures (this is why Lab 4’s bonus and Lab 6 use asm10). A third failure type in CrossMap’s code is Fail(Multiple_hits): the position maps to more than one place, as in repeats and duplicated regions; the PAF from minimap2 -cx asm5 includes secondary alignments. Answer Counted in calls_to_ref.bam (workshop cluster test run; the instructor’s separate alignment with bcftools mpileup gives the same counts) : at GPD2, XV:218,140, 27 reads cover the site: 22 carry T (the alternate base), 1 carries G (the reference base), 2 carry A and 2 carry C (22 of 27 = 82%). At ADH1, XV:159,763, 34 reads: 29 carry G (the alternate base) and 5 carry A (the reference base) (29 of 34 = 85%). So most reads support each variant, from about 27-34 reads in total. The few reads with another base are sequencing errors: these reads are about 87% accurate on average (they peak at Q9, Lab 3), which means about 13% of their bases are wrong, so even at a true variant 10-20% of the reads are expected to disagree. Question 12: The VCF genotype is GT=1 at both loci. Is this variant homozygous or heterozygous? Why is GT=1 the right model for this isolate, and what would you expect to see in the reads at a heterozygous site in a diploid? Answer Homozygous means both copies carry the same allele, heterozygous that they differ. BAL_1a is a homozygous diploid: the ScRAP strain table lists it as ploidy 2n and homozygous. It was grown from a single spore, and its two genome copies carry the same base at almost every site. So GT=1, a single alternate allele, is a fitting model, and medaka_variant is a haploid caller. In the reads such a site shows nearly all reads with the same base (here 82% and 85%; the rest are sequencing errors). A heterozygous site in a diploid would show two alleles at roughly half of the reads each; that is a pattern that medaka_variant cannot report. Question 13 (the real-variant question): For each of the two genes, look at the snpEff effect in the VCF record, the position of the variant in the gene track and the read support (Question 11). Explain why such a variant could matter. Look both genes up on SGD, and say what you would do next to find out whether the variant has an effect. Answer GPD2 / YOL059W (XV:218,140, G>T, QUAL 39). snpEff predicts stop_gained (HIGH), p.Glu339: the codon for amino acid 339 of 440 becomes a stop codon (your annotated.vcf, workshop cluster test run, 2026-10-18). The stop removes about the last 100 amino acids of the 440, so the protein is truncated and this could reduce GPD2 function. SGD S000005420 describes GPD2 as an NAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and reports that a deletion of the gene (gpd2*Δ) shows impaired anaerobic growth. So this is a variant in a gene associated with glycerol production and with growth without oxygen. GPD1 is a paralog of GPD2 (a related gene from an ancient duplication), so a loss of GPD2 may be partly covered by GPD1; the overall effect is not known. The read support is 22 of 27 reads (T), so the reads support the call well. Next to it, at 218,142, is a second change in the same codon (G>A, called ‘synonymous’ on its own). Together they make TAA, still a stop codon. snpEff judges each variant separately, so always look at neighbours. ADH1 / YOL086C (XV:159,763, A>G, QUAL 49). snpEff predicts missense_variant (MODERATE), p.Cys278Arg: amino acid 278 of 348 changes from cysteine to arginine (your annotated.vcf, workshop cluster test run, 2026-10-18). SGD S000005446 describes ADH1 as the fermentative alcohol dehydrogenase, which converts acetaldehyde to ethanol. This is a variant in a gene associated with fermentation. A missense variant could alter how the enzyme works, but MODERATE only means “changes the protein, effect unknown”: nothing here shows that it changes ethanol production. The read support is 29 of 34 reads (G). For both: we say “a variant in a gene associated with…”, not “the cause of” anything. The call is from a haploid model (GT=1), a fitting model because every copy of BAL_1a’s genome carries the same base (a homozygous diploid; ScRAP: 2n, homozygous), and the measured reads (82% and 85% carry the alternate base; the rest are sequencing errors of about 13% at Q9) fit a true variant. To test the effect you would need experiments, for example measuring growth or ethanol and glycerol production, or putting the variant in a reference strain. For the case: the wolf carries a predicted stop in GPD2 and a missense change in ADH1. These are differences in genes associated with fermentation. Whether they change how the wolf ferments is a hypothesis; measuring ethanol and glycerol would test it. Question 7 (the real-variant question): Look at the deletion, the genes it overlaps and CUP1-2 on SGD (S000001097). Explain why a change in the number of CUP1 copies could matter for a yeast strain. What is uncertain about exactly which sequence is missing? Answer What the data show. In the assembly of BAL_1a, a 2,000 bp stretch of the reference is missing at VIII:213,953-215,953 (SVIM-asm, svim_asm.DEL.95, ID in the workshop cluster test run). It lies 213,952 bp from the chromosome end, outside the rDNA, not near the end of a contig and with no Ty or LTR feature in it (sv_context.tsv). Why it could matter. SGD S000001097 describes CUP1-2 as a metallothionein that binds copper and mediates resistance to high concentrations of copper and cadmium, and says that the locus is variably amplified in different strains, with two copies, CUP1-1 and CUP1-2, in S288C. The reference has two tandem copies of an about 2 kb unit; this assembly has one unit fewer. A strain with fewer copies of a gene for copper and cadmium detoxification could tolerate less copper or cadmium, and a strain with more copies more. So this is a deletion in a gene associated with copper and cadmium resistance, a copy-number variant (CNV), a type of SV. The reads (Question 8) show the deletion in every read that spans the repeat, as expected for a homozygous diploid isolate (ScRAP: 2n, homozygous). Whether BAL_1a really is less tolerant is not known from this data; that needs a growth test on copper or cadmium. Nobody has shown here that this SV causes any phenotype. What is uncertain. In a tandem repeat, the repeat units are nearly identical, so the exact position of the missing unit is ambiguous: the caller places the deletion over CUP1-2 and about 770 bp into the 3′ end of RSC30 (the deletion ends at 215,953; RSC30 starts at 215,183), but any identical unit could be “the” missing one. Do not read this as RSC30 being truncated. The Ensembl/SGD description of YHR054C calls it a partial duplicate of RSC30, and it starts exactly 1,998 bp (one unit) before RSC30’s 3′ end, so each unit carries a copy of that RSC30 segment and the one remaining unit very likely keeps RSC30 intact. A second caution is that assemblers often collapse tandem repeats, so an assembly can have fewer copies than the real genome; the reads are the check (Question 8). For the case: the wolf has one CUP1 unit where the corgi has two: a deletion in a gene associated with copper and cadmium resistance. Whether the wolf tolerates less copper is a hypothesis; a growth test on copper would answer it. In IGV you see the same thing: staggered black deletion lines and a coverage dip (to about 6-18 reads) rather than a gap to zero. The isolate is a homozygous diploid (ScRAP: 2n, homozygous), and all spanning reads agree, so the data fit one unit fewer than in S288C. Question 10 (case review): In three sentences, what did you learn about the wolf compared with the corgi, and what can you not conclude from one wild strain and one lab strain? When you have written your answer, the instructor will show the case-review slide. Answer A model answer, one point per sentence: What we learned. The wolf’s (BAL_1a) reads were good enough to use (Lab 3) and gave an assembly of about 18 contigs with 99.7% of BUSCO genes complete (Lab 4). It differs from the corgi (S288C) at roughly 1% of its bases (Lab 5), including a predicted stop in GPD2 and a missense change in ADH1, both genes associated with fermentation; it carries one CUP1 unit fewer than S288C, in a gene associated with copper and cadmium resistance, and lacks Ty elements that S288C carries (Lab 6). ScRAP reports 98.49% identity between this isolate’s assembly and the reference (about 1.5% difference): the same order of magnitude as our rough estimate, though the two numbers are measured differently. What we cannot conclude. These are candidate differences, not causes: they do not show that the wolf ferments differently or tolerates less copper. With one wild strain and one lab strain we cannot tell a lab or wild adaptation from a difference that is private to one strain or neutral. And neither strain is “pure”: about 88% of S288C descends from a wild fig isolate (EM93), and the wolf has been grown in labs since it was collected. Next steps. Test growth on copper and measure ethanol and glycerol; compare more strains; and check the small indels with the Illumina run of the same sample, ERR8603864 (paired-end, 150-bp reads), because nanopore indel calls are the least trustworthy kind (Lab 5). What you learned: SVs are differences of 50 bp or more. An assembly-based caller such as SVIM-asm finds them from the alignment of the assembly to the reference, and reports types, sizes and coordinates in a VCF. Most SVs are small (under 500 bp), a cluster near 5.9 kb points to Ty elements, and a deletion in a tandem repeat such as CUP1 changes a gene’s copy number. A call is a hypothesis: check it against the reads, and say “a deletion in a gene associated with…”, not “the cause of”.
